<explanation>
Based on your project's file tree and README, Kingfisher is clearly a Swift-based image downloading and caching library. It is designed to provide an easy-to-use, asynchronous API for working with remote images (including image processing and caching) while supporting multiple platforms (iOS, macOS, tvOS, watchOS, and even SwiftUI).

Below is a step-by-step explanation on how to draw a detailed system design diagram for Kingfisher:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Library Core – This includes all the central functionality found under the Sources directory. Key subcomponents are:
       - Cache: (Sources/Cache) manages both memory and disk cache.
       - Networking: (Sources/Networking) contains the image downloader, request modifiers, retry strategies, session delegates, etc.
       - Image Processing & Formats: (Sources/Image) where image processors, filters, and image format handling are implemented.
       - General Utilities: (Sources/General) holds main Kingfisher APIs (KF.swift, KingfisherManager.swift, options, etc.).
       - Extensions & Integration: (Sources/Extensions, Sources/SwiftUI, Sources/Views) that expose the convenient methods for UIKit/AppKit, SwiftUI views, and more.
       - Utility Helpers: (Sources/Utility) containing helper classes like callback queues, result types, and simple delegates.

2. Include Demo & CI/CD Environment:
   • Demo(s) – The Demo directory contains multiple platform-specific demonstration apps (iOS, macOS, tvOS, watchOS) which illustrate how Kingfisher’s components are integrated into real applications.
   • CI/CD Pipelines – The presence of a .github folder (with workflows for building and testing) and fastlane configuration indicates automation for building, testing, and releasing the library.

3. Identify External Components and Testing:
   • Testing – The Tests directory shows how unit tests cover each major module (e.g., caching, downloading, image processing, extensions). The project also includes a dependency on Nocilla for stubbing network requests.
   • Package Managers – Files like Gemfile, Podspec, and Package.swift point to integration with CocoaPods, Swift Package Manager, and even Ruby-based automation tools.

4. How to Represent Relationships & Workflow:
   • Create distinct boxes for each major component (Core, Cache, Networking, Image Processing, UI Extensions, Utilities).
   • Draw arrows from UI and API layers (UIKit/SwiftUI Extensions) toward the Core.
       - Image requests initiated from UI components pass into the Kingfisher API.
       - The Kingfisher Manager (or the KF builder) triggers the Networking layer to download images.
       - Downloaded images pass through the Image Processing Pipeline (chaining processors such as Downsampling or RoundCorner) before being sent to the Cache.
       - Requests for the same image then might be served directly from the Memory or Disk Cache.
   • Add directional arrows that highlight data flow:
       - From the application’s image view (via kf extension or KF builder syntax) to the Kingfisher API.
       - From the API to Networking & Cache, then back to the UI.
   • Use annotations to indicate that processors can be chained, and that cancellation and indicator support is also built-in.

5. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   • Modularity and Independent Components: Each module (downloader, cache, networking, image processor) works independently and can be used separately if needed.
   • Extensibility: The project provides extension points (for UI components and network request modifications) to easily plug in custom behavior.
   • Reuse & Composition: The use of method chaining (as seen in the advanced examples) shows a composable design—this can be depicted as a pipeline for image processing.
   • Cross-Platform Support: The diagram should include labeled sections (or different colored shapes) indicating support for UIKit, AppKit, SwiftUI, etc.

6. Diagram Presentation Guidelines:
   • Clearly label each box—for example, “Cache System (Memory & Disk)”, “Image Downloader”, “Image Processing Pipeline”, “Kingfisher Manager”, “UI Extensions (UIButton, UIImageView, SwiftUI KFImage)”, “Utilities & Helpers”, “Demo Applications”, “CI/CD & Testing”.
   • Use directional arrows to indicate data flow:
       - For instance, “Request initiated” arrow from UI Extensions → Kingfisher Manager.
       - “Download and Process image” arrows among Downloader, Processors, and Cache.
       - “Return cached image” arrow from Cache back to UI.
   • Apply color coding or distinct shapes to denote different categories. For example:
       - Rectangles for core components.
       - Rounded boxes for UI extensions.
       - Cloud or cylinder icons for external systems (like disk storage or CI/CD pipelines).
   • Include a legend if necessary that explains symbols, colors, and arrow types (request flow versus dependency relationships).

7. Tailoring the Diagram to this Project Type:
   • Since Kingfisher is a pure library (an open-source tool), emphasize its independence and how the individual components (networking, caching, processing) can be extended or used separately.
   • Make sure that the diagram clearly demonstrates the layered architecture:
       1. API & Core Logic at the center.
       2. Service layers (cache, networking) as supporting services.
       3. Integration layers (extensions) interfacing with external frameworks (UIKit, SwiftUI).
   • Highlight integration aspects in demo applications since there is robust support for different platforms.
   • For unit testing and CI/CD, you can show these as side modules that “validate” the core components, using arrows to depict testing flows.

By following these instructions and leveraging the detailed file structure information along with the README content, you can create a comprehensive diagram that:
   • Clearly indicates the flow from the image view setup (via the kf extension or KF builder) to the actual downloading, processing, caching, and then back to the UI.
   • Illustrates all the underlying modules that make Kingfisher modular, extensible, and highly reusable.
   • Provides sufficient annotations with names, roles, and interactions so that even a principal software engineer can quickly grasp the design principles and architecture behind Kingfisher.

This detailed, component-driven diagram will not only help in understanding the overall structure of Kingfisher but also serve as excellent documentation for collaboration and future development efforts.
</explanation>
